newsitem.title: INDIA: India panel recommends derivatives, share buybacks.
newsitem.headline: India panel recommends derivatives, share buybacks.

text.p: A blue-ribbon panel on Monday recommended sweeping changes in laws governing Indian firms, saying some of them were "antiquated".
It also suggested that Indian companies move towards issuing a range of new financial instruments, and laid down guidelines that would let firms buy back their own shares.

"The main objective of the group was to rewrite the Companies Act to facilitate a healthy growth of the Indian corporate sector under a liberalised, fast-changing and highly competitive environment," the report said.
It suggested that domestic companies should be allowed to issue derivatives, options and quasi-equity instruments.
"Indian companies should be enabled to issue hybrids, derivatives, options, as well as shares and quasi-equity instruments with differential rights," the report said.
It said hybrids were a combination of securities including their derivatives or options. "Shares with differential rights" refer to differing voting and dividend rights.
Even as the working group, set up by the government, released its report, global investment bank Lehman Brothers said it saw India's debt market developing and forecast the evolution of derivatives.
"The development of a debt market will provide an alternate route to funds," C. Daniel Tyree, chairman of Lehman Brothers Asia, told a news conference.
"As Indian capital markets open up, swaps will develop and eventually futures and options will emerge."

The panel's report recommended that foreign companies be allowed to issue Indian depositary receipts (IDRs) on the lines of European global depositary receipts (GDRs) where the underlying security is the equity or any other security of the foreign company.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram set up the working group last year under the chairmanship of K.R. Chandratre, the then chairman of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India to present a report for public debate.
The group said it favoured allowing companies to buy back their own shares subject to certain conditions.
"In today's context, the group strongly believes this section (of the Act) is antiquated, and goes against the long-term interests of corporate sector growth and shareholder value," the report said.
It recommended that shareholders must approve a proposed buyback through a special resolution which states the amount allocated, and the time frame, for the buyback.
The funds allocated for the buyback must be from the firm's "free reserves" and share premium account, the report said.
Firms which have issued shares at a premium to their face value usually deposit the funds in a separate account.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in his budget proposals for 1997/98 (April-March) said last week that buybacks of shares would be allowed under a new company law for which a legislative bill would be introduced in parliament.
The group said companies must not be allowed to issue any new shares -- including rights shares but excluding bonus shares -- for one year after the buyback was completed.
"Since a buyback is for extinguishing share capital it should not lead to an increase in the debt-equity ratio in excess of 2:1," the report said.

It said in the case of a buyback that would constitute a treasury operation, new shares should not be re-issued for a period of two years. If a company's treasury department bought its own shares as an investment it would qualify as a treasury operation.
